title: RBAC Overview
description: Learn how Azure Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) limits what identities can do in Azure.

data.text: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) is Azure's system for managing who can do what. Instead of giving everyone admin access, you assign roles that match exactly the permissions needed for a job.
RBAC has three main parts: the security principal (who), the role definition (what they can do), and the scope (where the permissions apply).

data.title: RBAC Components
items: Security Principal — user, group, service principal, or managed identity
Role Definition — a collection of permissions like Reader, Contributor, or Owner
Scope — management group, subscription, resource group, or single resource
Role Assignment — the link that ties a principal to a role at a scope

data.title: Assign RBAC Role with Azure CLI
data.content: Grant a service principal Contributor access to a resource group.
data.code: az role assignment create   --assignee "service-principal-object-id"   --role Contributor   --resource-group myResourceGroup

data.title: Best Practice
data.text: Follow the principle of least privilege. Give the minimum permissions needed. You can always grant more later.

A role assignment is the combination of three things: a security principal (who), a role definition (what actions are allowed), and a scope (where). Azure evaluates all role assignments that apply to a resource and grants the union of their permissions. There is no implicit deny: if any assignment allows an action, the action is allowed unless a deny assignment blocks it.

data.title: Assign a data-plane role to a managed identity
data.content: Use the principal ID (object ID) of the identity, not its client ID. Add --assignee-principal-type to avoid a slow directory lookup.
data.code:
principalId=$(az webapp identity show -g rg-shop -n shop-api --query principalId -o tsv)
storageId=$(az storage account show -g rg-shop -n shopstorage --query id -o tsv)

az role assignment create \
  --assignee-object-id "$principalId" \
  --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal \
  --role "Storage Blob Data Reader" \
  --scope "$storageId"

# Verify what the identity can do
az role assignment list --assignee "$principalId" --all -o table

data.text: This distinction trips up almost everyone. Contributor on a storage account lets you manage the account (networking, replication, keys) but does not let you read blob data. Reading blobs requires a data-plane role such as Storage Blob Data Reader. The same split exists for Key Vault (Key Vault Secrets User), Service Bus (Azure Service Bus Data Receiver), and Cosmos DB (Cosmos DB Built-in Data Contributor).

rows: Create or delete a storage account

data.title: What interviewers look for
data.text: Explain that RBAC is additive and inherited, and that control-plane roles do not grant data-plane access. If asked to debug "the app has Contributor but still gets 403", the answer is almost always a missing data-plane role, a firewall or private endpoint, or a token issued for the wrong audience.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: RBAC controls access with roles, not individual permissions.
Scope limits where a role applies.
Use least privilege — start with Reader, add permissions only when needed.
